definition: A spectral envelope is the overall shape that sets how strong the different frequency components of a sound are. In the Shepard tones described here, it is a fixed bell-shaped pattern centered on a particular frequency range, which changes the tones’ spectral similarity and can influence pitch judgments.

reasons: The claim that the spectral envelope "changes the tones’ spectral similarity" is not directly supported by the packet; the packet says Shepard tones are generated under fixed bell-shaped spectral envelopes and discusses spectrally similar/dissimilar adaptor-target combinations, but does not state that the envelope itself changes spectral similarity.
The definition adds a causal influence on pitch judgments that is only partly supported in this packet and should not be generalized beyond the specific Shepard-tone experiment described.

The definition claims the spectral envelope “changes the tones’ spectral similarity”; the packet discusses “spectrally consistent (A3–A3, C6–C6) and inconsistent (A3–C6, C6–A3) adaptor-target combinations,” but it does not state that the envelope specifically changes “spectral similarity.”

The packet supports that Shepard tones use a “fixed bell-shaped spectral envelope” centered at particular frequencies (A3 and C6) to generate component amplitudes, and that this relates to pitch/judgment effects (e.g., relative pitch height judgments). However, because the “spectral similarity” claim is not explicitly supported, the full definition cannot be accepted.
